status: drafted via lean single-pass workflow grounded in the real extracted verse text
notes: Read the full Ethiopian-translation text of Amos (9 chapters, 146 verses) directly from amos_49.json before drafting - it is textually identical to KJV throughout (same phrasing, same 'for three transgressions...and for four' refrain eight times, same plumbline/summer-fruit/altar visions, same Amaziah confrontation, same closing restoration oracle at 9:11-15 quoted by James in Acts 15). No real content differences from the standard 66-book canon found for this book (unlike Ezra elsewhere in this same Ethiopian translation) - Amos is shared-canon content, so this draft adapts the already-validated KJV Amos structure (2 person-tier managers + 4 law/theme tiers) almost exactly, re-verified line-by-line against this translation's own extracted text rather than assumed. All character ids suffixed '_ethiopian' to avoid collision with the existing KJV Amos.json ids. Structure: Amos himself (manager, personally intercedes twice in 7:1-6 and is later confronted by Amaziah), Amaziah the priest of Bethel (manager, promoted from a background figure since he has his own confrontation scene, quoted dialogue, and a personally-named judgment oracle against his household in 7:16-17 - removing him would remove the book's one dialogic scene, satisfying rule 3), and four law/theme tiers covering the book's major structural units: Oracles Against the Nations (1:3-2:16, the eight-nation indictment climaxing on Israel), Social Injustice & False Worship (3:1-6:14, why judgment falls - corrupt courts, luxury, empty ritual), Visions of Judgment (7:7-9:4, the three unaverted visions - plumbline, summer fruit, the altar - distinct from the two earlier visions Amos personally averted by intercession), and Restoration of David's Fallen Booth (9:11-15, the closing reversal into hope). No submanagers - no minor named individual in this book supports a major figure closely enough to warrant promotion; Uzziah and Jeroboam II are cited only as chronological/reported markers (they never speak or act on-page) so they are folded into Amos's and Amaziah's own verse notes rather than given separate entries, matching the KJV precedent. NAMING-COLLISION FLAGS (same as KJV, re-verified against this text): Uzziah (1:1) is the same king called Azariah elsewhere - one man, two names, not two kings; Jeroboam 'the son of Joash' (1:1) is Jeroboam II, distinct from the earlier Jeroboam I son of Nebat who founded Israel's rival worship system at Bethel - both are called bare 'Jeroboam' elsewhere; 'house of Isaac' (7:16) and 'high places of Isaac' (7:9) are poetic names for the nation of Israel, not the patriarch Isaac of Genesis appearing in person; 'tabernacle of David' (9:11) is a dynastic reference to the fallen Davidic royal line, not the person of David from Samuel/Kings/Chronicles/Psalms appearing on-page. KJV/Ethiopian spelling preserved exactly as extracted, including 'sycomore' (not 'sycamore') at 7:14 and 'grasshoppers' (not 'locusts') at 7:1 - the source text's own word choice, not a synonym substitution.

characters.name: Amos

verses.note: Superscription: 'The words of Amos, who was among the herdman of Tekoa... in the days of Uzziah king of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash king of Israel, two years before the earthquake.' Naming flag: Uzziah is the same king called Azariah elsewhere - one man, two names. Naming flag: 'Jeroboam the son of Joash' is Jeroboam II, distinct from the earlier Jeroboam I son of Nebat.
Opening theophany: 'The LORD will roar from Zion, and utter his voice from Jerusalem: and the habitations of the shepherds shall mourn, and the top of Carmel shall wither.'

Not present as a standalone unit in the extracted text's chapter 7 (which opens directly at the grasshopper/fire vision text corresponding to KJV 7:1-3, 4-6) - Amos personally intercedes twice and judgment is averted both times: pleading over the grasshoppers ('O Lord GOD, forgive, I beseech thee: by whom shall Jacob arise? for he is small' - 'The LORD repented for this: It shall not be'), then over the fire vision ('cease, I beseech thee... This also shall not be, saith the Lord GOD'). His most personally dialogic exchange with God in the book.

Answering Amaziah: 'I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son: but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit: And the LORD took me as I followed the flock, and the LORD said unto me, Go, prophesy unto my people Israel.'

Pronounces personal judgment on Amaziah directly in response to being ordered to stop prophesying, quoting Amaziah's own words back first: 'drop not thy word against the house of Isaac' - a poetic name for Israel, not the patriarch Isaac appearing in person.

funFacts: The only writing prophet who identifies himself solely by trade and hometown rather than lineage - a herdman of Tekoa and gatherer of sycomore fruit (1:1; 7:14) - and uses that fact himself as proof his call came from God, not prophetic training.
From Tekoa in Judah but sent north to prophesy against Israel's royal sanctuary at Bethel - a foreign critic in his audience's eyes.
Twice personally averts coming judgment through intercession (7:1-6) before the vision cycle shifts to three final, unaverted visions (see Visions of Judgment).

characters.name: Amaziah

verses.note: Reports Amos to the king: 'Amaziah the priest of Bethel sent to Jeroboam king of Israel, saying, Amos hath conspired against thee in the midst of the house of Israel: the land is not able to bear all his words.' Naming flag: this Jeroboam is Jeroboam II (1:1), not Jeroboam I son of Nebat.

Confronts Amos directly: 'O thou seer, go, flee thee away into the land of Judah, and there eat bread, and prophesy there: But prophesy not again any more at Bethel: for it is the king's chapel, and it is the king's court.'

Quoted back by Amos before the judgment oracle: 'Thou sayest, Prophesy not against Israel, and drop not thy word against the house of Isaac.' Naming flag: 'house of Isaac' is a poetic name for Israel, not the patriarch Isaac of Genesis.

funFacts: Priest of Bethel - Israel's royal sanctuary, not Jerusalem's temple - a state religious official, not an independent figure (7:10).
The only person in Amos who directly confronts the prophet and receives a named, personal judgment oracle in return (7:16-17).

characters.name: Oracles Against the Nations
characters.purpose: A rhetorical trap opening the book - Amos indicts Israel's neighbors and Judah one by one for their own well-known atrocities, letting the audience agree before the same 'for three transgressions...and for four' formula lands, unavoidably, on Israel itself (2:6-16), the true target of the whole sequence.

verses.note: Damascus/Syria judged 'because they have threshed Gilead with threshing instruments of iron'; fire sent into 'the house of Hazael,' devouring 'the palaces of Ben-hadad'; captivity to Kir.
Gaza/Philistia judged 'because they carried away captive the whole captivity, to deliver them up to Edom.'
Tyrus judged 'because they delivered up the whole captivity to Edom, and remembered not the brotherly covenant.'
Edom judged 'because he did pursue his brother with the sword, and did cast off all pity, and his anger did tear perpetually.'
Ammon judged 'because they have ripped up the women with child of Gilead, that they might enlarge their border.'
Moab judged 'because he burned the bones of the king of Edom into lime.'
Judah judged 'because they have despised the law of the LORD, and have not kept his commandments, and their lies caused them to err.'
Israel judged 'because they sold the righteous for silver, and the poor for a pair of shoes' - the longest and climactic oracle, the true target the earlier seven built toward.

funFacts: Uses the identical 'for three transgressions...and for four' refrain eight times running, so listeners are agreeing with judgment on their enemies before the formula turns on them.

characters.name: Social Injustice & False Worship
characters.purpose: Details exactly why judgment falls on Israel: exploitation of the poor, corrupt courts, luxury built on oppression, and empty ritual worship offered without justice - 'let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream' (5:24) is the book's own summary of what is missing.

verses.note: 'You only have I known of all the families of the earth: therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities' - election creates accountability, not exemption.
'Hear this word, ye kine of Bashan, that are in the mountain of Samaria, which oppress the poor, which crush the needy' - addressed to Samaria's wealthy women.
'Prepare to meet thy God, O Israel' - closing refrain of a chapter cataloguing ignored warnings (famine, drought, blight, pestilence, overthrow like Sodom and Gomorrah, 4:6-11).
'They afflict the just, they take a bribe, and they turn aside the poor in the gate from their right' - corrupt courts named directly.
'Woe unto you that desire the day of the LORD!... the day of the LORD is darkness, and not light' - the expected day of vindication reversed into judgment.

'I hate, I despise your feast days... take thou away from me the noise of thy songs... but let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream' - ritual worship rejected without justice behind it.
Those 'that lie upon beds of ivory... but they are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph' - luxury indicted for its indifference.

funFacts: 'Kine of Bashan' (4:1) compares Samaria's wealthy women to the fattened cattle of Bashan's rich pastureland - one of the most memorable insults in prophetic literature.

characters.name: Visions of Judgment
characters.purpose: Where the first two visions of the cycle (grasshoppers, fire, covered under Amos's own entry) were turned aside by Amos's intercession, these three - plumbline, summer fruit, and the altar - are not: judgment moves from a warning that could still be averted to a sentence declared final.

verses.note: Plumbline vision: 'Behold, the Lord stood upon a wall made by a plumbline, with a plumbline in his hand... I will set a plumbline in the midst of my people Israel: I will not again pass by them any more.' Naming flag: 'the high places of Isaac' is a poetic name for Israel. Naming flag: 'the house of Jeroboam' here is Jeroboam II, not Jeroboam I son of Nebat.
Basket of summer fruit vision: 'The end is come upon my people of Israel; I will not again pass by them any more.'

Within the same vision unit: dishonest trade indicted - 'making the ephah small, and the shekel great, and falsifying the balances by deceit... that we may buy the poor for silver, and the needy for a pair of shoes.'

Vision of the LORD standing upon the altar, commanding the posts struck so they shake: 'he that fleeth of them shall not flee away, and he that escapeth of them shall not be delivered' - no intercession is recorded here, unlike the first two visions.

funFacts: The plumbline vision gives the book its most enduring image - Israel tested against a fixed, unmovable standard.

characters.name: Restoration of David's Fallen Booth
characters.purpose: After nine chapters of near-unrelieved judgment, the book ends on a sudden reversal - a promise to raise up the fallen tabernacle (booth) of David, rebuild ruined cities, and restore agricultural abundance - so a book that opened with the LORD roaring in judgment (1:2) closes with unconditional hope.

verses.note: 'In that day will I raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen, and close up the breaches thereof; and I will raise up his ruins, and I will build it as in the days of old.' Naming flag: 'David' here is a dynastic reference to the fallen Davidic line, not the person of David appearing on-page.

'The plowman shall overtake the reaper... I will bring again the captivity of my people of Israel, and they shall build the waste cities, and inhabit them... and they shall no more be pulled up out of their land which I have given them, saith the LORD thy God.'

funFacts: Quoted directly by James at the Jerusalem council (Acts 15:16-17) as scriptural warrant for including Gentiles in the church.

genealogyLists.note: No bulk/unresolved genealogy references needed for this book - Amos gives no family lineage for himself or Amaziah, and the only other named/quasi-named figures (Uzziah, Jeroboam II) are folded into the manager entries above as chronological markers rather than treated as separate characters.
